To grease someone's palm means to bribe someone — to secretly give a person money (or something valuable) so they will do something for you, usually something they are not supposed to do, or to make them do their job faster and in your favor.

Think of it this way: you are "slipping money into someone's hand" to buy their cooperation, loyalty, or silence. It almost always involves dishonesty or corruption at some level.
The Literal Image Behind It

The word "grease" here is used as a verb, meaning to make something move smoothly. Just like you put grease on a squeaky door hinge to make it open without friction, you put money into someone's palm (their hand) to make a situation "run smoothly" — to remove obstacles, speed things up, or get a favorable outcome.

So the idiom paints a very vivid picture: money = grease, the person's hand = the machine, and the bribe = the lubricant that makes things work in your favor.
Origin and History

This idiom is very old. It dates back to at least the 16th century in English literature. The idea of comparing a bribe to grease is ancient because greasing mechanical parts to make them move was a well-known concept. People simply applied that logic to human behavior — just as machines need grease to function, corrupt officials and gatekeepers "need" money to do what you want.

The word "palm" refers to the inner surface of the hand, the place where money is most naturally and discreetly passed from one person to another. This makes the image even more precise — it is not just giving money openly, it is slipping it into the palm, which suggests secrecy.
How It Is Used

The idiom is typically used in situations where:

  • A bureaucrat or official demands or expects a secret payment to process your paperwork, approve your application, or look the other way.
  • Someone pays a security guard, border official, or gatekeeper to let them through without following the rules.
  • A business entity pays a politician or judge to receive favorable decisions.
  • Someone is trying to get a service faster than normal by paying someone unofficially "under the table."

The key elements almost always present are: secrecy, unfairness, and an unofficial exchange.
Example Sentences

Here are several examples so you can see how this idiom works naturally in real speech and writing:

  1. "The contractor greased the inspector's palm, so the building passed inspection even though it had several violations."
    → The contractor bribed the inspector to ignore the problems.
  2. "In some countries, you have to grease a few palms just to get a business license approved."
    → You have to bribe officials to get basic government services.
  3. "He greased the doorman's palm with a hundred-dollar bill to get a table at the fully-booked restaurant."
    → He bribed the doorman with money to secure a reserved spot.
  4. "I refuse to grease anyone's palm. If I can't get it honestly, I won't get it at all."
    → The speaker refuses to offer bribes on principle.
  5. "The deal went through suspiciously fast — someone must have greased a few palms along the way."
    → Someone likely bribed people to speed up the process.
The Tone of This Idiom

This idiom carries a negative moral tone. It implies wrongdoing, corruption, and dishonesty. When you say someone "greased a palm," you are suggesting that something unfair or unethical took place. It is not a neutral expression.

However, the tone can be:

  • Accusatory — "He greased the judge's palm." (a direct accusation)
  • Matter-of-fact or cynical — "That's just how it works there; you grease a few palms and move on." (sadly accepting corruption as a reality)
  • Self-righteous or principled — "I'd never grease someone's palm." (expressing moral opposition)
Variations of the Idiom

The idiom has a few close relatives you should know:

  • "Grease the wheels" — This is slightly different. It means to make a process run more smoothly in general, not necessarily through bribery. It can sometimes be used in a neutral or even positive sense. "A few kind words can really grease the wheels of a negotiation."
  • "Oil someone's palm" — Exact same meaning as grease someone's palm. Oil and grease are interchangeable here since both are lubricants. This variation is less common today but still understood.
  • "Crossed someone's palm with silver" — An older, more poetic version meaning the same thing — giving money to someone (silver coins historically). Today this phrase is sometimes used humorously.
Similar Idioms With Related Meanings

Knowing these will help round out your understanding of the world of bribery-related language:

  • "Pay under the table" — To pay someone secretly, outside of official records, often to avoid taxes or rules. Very similar meaning to greasing a palm.
  • "Sweeten the deal" — To add extra incentives (not always through bribery; can be legitimate) to make someone more willing to agree.
  • "Buy someone off" — To pay a person to stop opposing you or to gain their silence or cooperation.
  • "In someone's pocket" — If an official is "in your pocket," it means you have already bribed or corrupted them to the point where they do whatever you want.
Is It Formal or Informal?

This idiom sits in the informal to semi-formal range. You would use it in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Journalism and news reporting (when describing corruption)
  • Novels, films, and storytelling
  • Casual essays or opinion pieces

You would not typically use it in a formal legal document or academic paper. In those contexts, you would instead say "bribery," "corrupt payment," or "illicit payment."
One Thing People Sometimes Get Wrong

Some learners think "grease someone's palm" can refer to any kind of gift or favor. It cannot. The idiom specifically implies a payment made to gain an unfair or dishonest advantage. A birthday gift, a tip at a restaurant, or a bonus paid to a hard-working employee are not examples of greasing a palm, because those are honest, open, and morally acceptable exchanges.

The moment an exchange becomes secret, corrupt, and aimed at bending rules, that is when this idiom applies.
Quick Summary

Core meaningTo bribe someone with money to get a favor, speed up a process, or gain an unfair advantage
ToneNegative — implies corruption and dishonesty
RegisterInformal to semi-formal
Key imageSlipping money secretly into someone's open palm

"Grease someone's palm" is one of the English language's most vivid and enduring idioms because the image it creates — quietly pressing money into a waiting hand — perfectly captures the sneaky, oily nature of bribery itself.
